title: Episode 104: Trending — Recommendations for the use of hormone and nonhormone treatment of vasomotor symptoms of menopause: Menopause Medical Eligibility Criteria (MenoMEC) based on insights from a modified Delphi panel
itunes_title: Trending — Recommendations for the use of hormone and nonhormone treatment of vasomotor symptoms of menopause: Menopause Medical Eligibility Criteria (MenoMEC) based on insights from a modified Delphi panel
description:
**Top Trending Friday** — our weekly pick of the most-discussed paper on PubMed this week.

**[Recommendations for the use of hormone and nonhormone treatment of vasomotor symptoms of menopause: Menopause Medical Eligibility Criteria (MenoMEC) based on insights from a modified Delphi panel](https://doi.org/10.1097/GME.0000000000002947)**

*Menopause, 2026*

DOI: [10.1097/GME.0000000000002947](https://doi.org/10.1097/GME.0000000000002947)

**Question:** Can a US expert panel agree which hormone and nonhormone treatments for menopausal hot flashes suit women with specific comorbidities?

**Answer:** A 15-physician modified Delphi (11 answered the survey; consensus at ≥70% agreement) built a 1–4 eligibility grid. Online, no comorbidity reached consensus on hormone versus nonhormone therapy; all were settled in person, with no vote tallies reported.

**Three takeaways**

1. Measured agreement covers the uncontroversial: hormone therapy first-line when safe, clonidine unanimously rejected; SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin, oxybutynin and NK-targeted drugs as alternatives.
2. Hormone-or-not for every listed comorbidity missed the 70% bar online; the in-person resolution is expert judgment with no tallies reported.
3. The contraceptive-style grid separates initiation from continuation and relative from absolute risk, so prior VTE is no longer an automatic no.

source_metadata.abstract:
Objectives:
                    To develop a Menopause Medical Eligibility Criteria (MenoMEC) tool to guide individualized, evidence-based care for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms due to menopause.
                  
                  
                    Methods:
                    We conducted a modified Delphi panel of 15 multidisciplinary experts to establish US-focused consensus recommendations for hormone and nonhormone therapy use in managing moderate-severe vasomotor symptoms, considering various comorbid conditions. An online survey assessed agreement with proposed recommendations using a nine-point Likert scale, with ≥70% agreement defining consensus. Items lacking consensus were discussed in a structured in-person meeting, leading to refined recommendations and final development of the tool.
                  
                  
                    Results:
                    Panelists affirmed hormone therapy as first-line for eligible women and nonhormone therapy for those with contraindications or who decline hormone therapy. Recommended first-line nonhormone therapy options were selective serotonin/serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin, and oxybutynin, after accounting for contraindications. Neurokinin therapies (eg, fezolinetant, elinzanetant) were supported as first-line but limited by access and cost. Clonidine and most herbal/over-the-counter products were not recommended due to potential adverse effects, drug-drug interactions, or lack of evidence of benefit or harm. Specific recommendations regarding the appropriateness of therapy addressed women with cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, thrombosis, liver disease, smoking, and hormone-sensitive cancers. All panelists agreed that there was an urgent need to provide structured guidance to the clinical community regarding the selection and use of hormone versus nonhormone therapy.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions:
                    This panel provided structured, symptom-based, and comorbidity-based recommendations to optimize therapy for the management of vasomotor symptoms and supported the development of a MenoMEC guideline for use in primary care clinical settings.
